title: When Commercial Customers Ask for AP Help, What Should Their Bank Be Ready to Offer?
summary: Learn what banks should offer when commercial clients ask for AP help, from vendor enablement and payment controls to reconciliation and support.
body_markdown:
*A practical guide to discovery questions, core capabilities and partner governance for banks responding to commercial AP requests*


A commercial customer may not walk into a bank asking for “vendor payment automation.” The request is more likely to sound practical:


- Can you help us stop cutting so many checks?


- Can you reduce the time our team spends following up with vendors?


- Can you give us a clearer view of what has been paid and what still needs attention?


Those questions create an important opening for commercial banks.


[The Association for Financial Professionals reports](https://www.financialprofessionals.org/training-resources/resources/survey-research-economic-data/Details/digitalpayments)


that 76% of surveyed organizations plan to update their payment strategy within the next three years, while checks still account for 26% of business-to-business payments.


A bank does not have to build and operate a complete accounts payable function to respond, but it does need to understand the customer’s operational problem, identify the capabilities that matter and offer a credible path forward.


## An AP Question Is a Relationship Signal


Commercial customers already look to their banks for support with cash management, payment activity and treasury operations. When a customer asks about AP modernization, the conversation is rarely limited to software. It can reveal pressure around staffing, check volume, vendor outreach, fraud controls, reconciliation or visibility across the payment process.


That makes the request a relationship signal. The bank that can help define the problem and guide the next step remains useful in a broader operating conversation, even when a specialized provider supplies part of the technology or service.


Research focused on small businesses reinforces the value of useful advice. In


[a recent J.D. Power study](https://www.jdpower.com/business/press-releases/2025-us-small-business-banking-satisfaction-study/)


,


61% of small businesses reported receiving financial advice from their bank and 94% of those recipients said the guidance positively influenced their financial habits. These findings should not be generalized to every commercial customer, but they show how proactive guidance can strengthen a banking relationship.


## Start by Defining What the Customer Means by AP Help


“AP automation” can describe several different functions. Some customers need help capturing invoices, routing approvals or managing purchase orders. Others have already approved the invoice and encounter friction when it is time to issue the payment.


For the second group, the core problem often sits between approval and reconciliation. The team may still print and mail checks, contact vendors about payment preferences, update bank details, respond to status questions, manage exceptions and match remittance information to the accounting record.


Relationship managers just need enough shared vocabulary to distinguish invoice workflow from vendor payment execution. That distinction keeps the conversation focused and helps the bank avoid recommending a larger system than the customer needs.


## Five Questions Relationship Managers Should Ask


A short discovery conversation can clarify the customer’s immediate need and expose the operational requirements behind it.


1. What does the current payment mix look like? Ask about check volume, electronic payments, urgent payments and any payment types that routinely create exceptions.


2. Which accounting or ERP system holds the approved payment information? The answer helps determine how instructions, statuses and reconciliation data should move between systems.


3. Who manages vendor enrollment and payment preferences? A digital payment method has limited value if the customer’s


staff must still contact every vendor and maintain every change.


4. Which approval, access and fraud controls are required? Clarify who can create, approve, release and review payments, along with how exceptions are escalated.


5. What reporting, reconciliation and support does the team need? Ask how the customer confirms payment status, handles remittance data, closes the books, and resolves vendor questions.


## What a Credible Commercial Banking AP Solution Should Include


A credible answer must cover more than the payment rail. ACH and virtual card capabilities matter, but the surrounding operating model determines whether the customer


actually reduces manual work.


[Nacha’s latest full-year figures show](https://www.nacha.org/content/business-business-b2b)


the scale of electronic B2B activity, with 8.08 billion ACH payments representing $63.11 trillion transferred. The growth of electronic payments does not eliminate the need to manage vendor adoption, controls, exceptions and usable payment data.


So, a credible commercial banking AP solution should include:


- Multiple payment methods that can accommodate vendor preferences and different payment use cases rather than forcing every transaction into one channel.


- Vendor enablement support that identifies payment preferences, assists with enrollment and maintains payment information.


- Connectivity with the customer’s accounting or ERP environment so approved payment instructions and status information can move through a controlled workflow.


-


Approval, access and fraud controls appropriate to the customer’s policies, including clear separation of duties and exception handling.


- Remittance data, realtime reporting and reconciliation support that give the AP team a usable record of payment activity.


- Implementation resources, ongoing service and defined escalation ownership for both customer


and vendor questions.


The bank should also be clear about scope. Vendor payment automation can digitize and manage approved payments and the work around them. It does not necessarily replace invoice capture, procurement or the customer’s accounting system.


## Use a Partner Without Outsourcing Accountability


A third-party model gives banks a practical alternative to building every component internally or sending the customer


away with a generic referral. The bank can extend its capabilities through an integrated or referral relationship while retaining an appropriate role in customer


communication and oversight.


That arrangement still requires governance.


[Federal Reserve guidance](https://www.federalreserve.gov/publications/2024-may-third-party-risk-management.htm)


for community banks states that using a third party


*does not* remove a bank’s responsibility to operate safely and comply with applicable requirements. It describes a risk management life cycle that includes planning, due diligence and selection, contract negotiation, ongoing monitoring and termination.


In practice, the bank should define the parties’ roles, data access, performance expectations, complaint handling, business continuity, escalation paths and exit options before presenting the capability to customers. Oversight should reflect the activity’s risk, complexity and importance to the customer


experience.


## Make the Handoff Feel Connected to the Bank


A referral can feel like abandonment when the customer


has to restart the conversation with a new provider. Relationship managers need a simple internal playbook that explains when to introduce the solution, what information to gather and who owns the next step.


The


customer


should understand who will manage implementation, vendor enrollment, service questions, and escalations.


The bank should also decide how relationship managers will receive updates and re-enter the conversation when broader treasury needs emerge.


This clarity matters as much as the technology. It helps the customer


move from an informal request to a defined evaluation process without losing continuity or accountability.

## Be Ready Before the Customer Asks


Commercial customers do not expect every bank to operate an AP platform. They do expect their bank to understand the problem well enough to recommend a credible next step.


Readiness starts with a practical discovery conversation, a clear definition of the capabilities the


customer needs


and a governed partner model that keeps the relationship connected. When those pieces are in place, an AP question becomes an opportunity to deliver useful guidance and expand the value of the treasury relationship.

## Frequently Asked Questions


### What is vendor payment automation for banks?


Vendor payment automation for banks is a capability a bank can offer directly, integrate with its services or provide through a referral. It digitizes approved vendor payments and supports related work such as vendor enrollment, payment controls, reporting and reconciliation.


### Why do commercial customers


ask their bank for AP help?


Commercial customers already rely on their bank for treasury services, cash management and payment activity. That makes the bank a natural starting point when a business wants to reduce paper checks, improve payment visibility or simplify vendor payment operations.


### Does a bank need to build AP automation in-house?


No. A bank can build a solution, integrate with a provider or make a referral based on its strategy and resources. When a third party is involved, the bank should apply appropriate due diligence, governance, monitoring and customer


service ownership.


### What should a commercial banking AP solution include?


A commercial banking AP solution should address payment methods, vendor enablement, accounting or ERP connectivity, approval and fraud controls, remittance data, reporting, reconciliation, implementation and ongoing support.


### How can banks help commercial customers


reduce paper checks?


Start by reviewing the customer’s payment mix and vendor acceptance. Eligible payments can then move to electronic methods such as ACH or virtual card while the operating model continues to support exceptions, vendor preferences and transactions that still require checks.
